en: Saṁyutta Nikāya 39.1 (SN 39.1, PTS SN iv 261) 1. Sāmaṇḍaka Chapter The Discourse to Sāmaṇḍaka At Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of ascetics. What five? (1) Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic holds such a doctrine and view as this: ‘Whatever a person experiences, whether it be pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, all that is caused by what was done in the past. This, bhikkhus, is called the first kind of ascetic. (2) Again, bhikkhus, some ascetic holds such a doctrine and view as this: ‘Whatever a person experiences, whether it be pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, all that is caused by a supreme being. This, bhikkhus, is called the second kind of ascetic. (3) Again, bhikkhus, some ascetic holds such a doctrine and view as this: ‘Whatever a person experiences, whether it be pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, all that is without cause or condition. This, bhikkhus, is called the third kind of ascetic. (4) Again, bhikkhus, some ascetic holds such a doctrine and view as this: ‘Whatever a person experiences, whether it be pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, all that is caused by the creative act of a self. This, bhikkhus, is called the fourth kind of ascetic. (5) Again, bhikkhus, some ascetic holds such a doctrine and view as this: ‘Whatever a person experiences, whether it be pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, all that is caused by the creative act of a self and by what was done in the past. This, bhikkhus, is called the fifth kind of ascetic. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of ascetics. Among these, bhikkhus, the ascetic who holds the view: ‘Whatever a person experiences, whether it be pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, all that is caused by what was done in the past’—if he is asked: ‘What is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of pleasure? he cannot answer. If he is asked: ‘What is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of pain? he cannot answer. If he is asked: ‘What is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling? he cannot answer. The ascetic who holds the view: ‘Whatever a person experiences... all that is caused by a supreme being’—if he is asked: ‘What is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of pleasure? he cannot answer... [and so on] ...he cannot answer. The ascetic who holds the view: ‘Whatever a person experiences... all that is without cause or condition’—if he is asked: ‘What is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of pleasure? he cannot answer... [and so on] ...he cannot answer. The ascetic who holds the view: ‘Whatever a person experiences... all that is caused by the creative act of a self’—if he is asked: ‘What is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of pleasure? he cannot answer... [and so on] ...he cannot answer. The ascetic who holds the view: ‘Whatever a person experiences... all that is caused by the creative act of a self and by what was done in the past’—if he is asked: ‘What is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of pleasure? he cannot answer... [and so on] ...he cannot answer. But, bhikkhus, when a Tathāgata appears in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Well-Farer, a Knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed guide for those to be tamed, a Teacher of gods and humans, an Awakened One, a Blessed One; when he teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and reveals the holy life in its fulfillment and purity; when a householder or a householder’s son hears that Dhamma and gains faith in the Tathāgata; when, having gained faith, he reflects thus: ‘Household life is crowded and dusty, the life gone forth is wide open. It is not easy, living the household life, to practice the holy life in its full perfection and purity as a polished shell. Suppose I shave off my hair and beard, put on the saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness. After some time, having abandoned a small or a large fortune, having abandoned a small or a large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the saffron robes, and goes forth from the household life into homelessness. Having thus gone forth, he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults. He trains himself by undertaking the training rules. He, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from taking life; with rod and weapon laid aside, gentle and kindly, he dwells compassionate toward all living beings.

Having abandoned the taking of what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; taking only what is given, expecting only what is given, by not stealing he dwells in purity. Having abandoned unchastity, he lives a life of celibacy, living apart, abstaining from sexual intercourse, the common person’s practice. Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech; he speaks truth, adheres to truth, is trustworthy and reliable, one who does not deceive the world. Having abandoned divisive speech, he abstains from divisive speech; he does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here in order to divide others from those here, nor does he repeat here what he has heard elsewhere in order to divide those from others. Thus, being a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of harmony, he delights in concord, enjoys concord, and speaks words that promote concord. Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech; he speaks words that are gentle, pleasing to the ear, lovable, words that go to the heart, courteous words that are dear and agreeable to many people. Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma and the Discipline; at the right time he speaks such words as are worth recording, reasonable, succinct, and beneficial. He, having abandoned the destruction of life, abstains from the destruction of life; with rod and weapon laid aside, gentle and kindly, he dwells compassionate toward all living beings. On one occasion the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling among the Vajjis at Ukkacelā on the bank of the river Gaṅgā.
Then the wanderer Sāmaṇḍaka approached the Venerable Sāriputta and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the wanderer Sāmaṇḍaka said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“‘Nibbāna, Nibbāna,’ friend Sāriputta, it is said.
What now, friend, is Nibbāna?
“That which, friend, is the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion—that is Nibbāna.”
“This is called Nibbāna.
“But, friend, is there a path, is there a way for the realization of this Nibbāna?
“There is indeed, friend, a path, there is a way for the realization of this Nibbāna.”
“But what, friends, is the path, what is the way for the realization of this Nibbāna?
“Friends, it is this very Noble Eightfold Path that is the way for the realization of this Nibbāna; that is to say:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.”
“This, friends, is the path, this is the way for the realization of this Nibbāna.
“Excellent, friend, is this path; excellent is this way for the realization of this Nibbāna.
And it is enough, friend Sāriputta, for diligence.”
First.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 39.16 (SN 39.16, PTS SN iv 262)
1. The Chapter on Sāmaṇḍaka. The Discourse on What is Difficult to Do:
“Friend Sāriputta, what indeed is difficult to do in this Dhamma and Vinaya?”
“Going forth, friend, is difficult in this Dhamma and Discipline.
“But once gone forth, friend, what is difficult?
“Once gone forth, friend, it is difficult to find delight.”
“But for one who delights [in the Dhamma], friend, what is difficult to do?
“For one who delights [in the Dhamma], friend, it is difficult to practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
“But how long, friend, must a bhikkhu who practices in accordance with the Dhamma be before he becomes an arahant?”
“Not long, friend.
The sixteenth.
(The summary is the same as the previous one.)
The Connected Discourses on Sāmaṇḍaka are complete.
